blocks.text: Africa is the province's nearest market and its steadiest. Namibia and Zimbabwe "add stability, repeat demand and counter-seasonal volume" (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p14). Regional trips are shorter in lead time and easier to convert, which helps the green season (Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p31). Africa is therefore both a base to keep and a market to grow (section 2.2).

The opportunity to 2035 is premium growth on top of that base. Nigerian and Ghanaian visitors spend as much per visit as visitors from the mature markets, from a far smaller base (section 2.2). Cape Town is not a cold start in Nigeria or Kenya, where awareness of South Africa exists and needs converting rather than building from scratch (Skift African Market Analysis, 16 Mar 2026, s4.2, s5).

Access is the constraint. Routes to Luanda, Maputo, Gaborone, Harare and Mauritius run above 80% load, so added demand there meets full aircraft (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "Seasonality"). Visas add friction: the CTICC reports that regional African event demand is constrained by visa requirements (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p45).

Africa holds two different markets. A Southern African base delivers volume, while Nigeria and Kenya offer premium demand from a large addressable pool. Three cautions apply. Nigeria and Ghana have no row in the growth model, so no 2035 arrivals figure exists for the two highest-spending African markets [Nigeria and Ghana arrivals targets: not modelled; Wesgro Research to add both]. Ghana sits in the watch tier for brand seeding rather than conversion (Skift African Market Analysis, 16 Mar 2026, s5). And regional travellers tend to stop in Johannesburg rather than continue to Cape Town (Stakeholder Insights Report, Mar 2026, p35).

Wesgro should run Africa as two markets: a regional volume base held through capacity and value, and a premium growth market in Nigeria and Kenya won through conversion. Nigeria is the priority for luxury, status-driven and conference travel. Kenya is the priority for business mobility and premium urban breaks, and both are reached through premium activation and the trade (Skift African Market Analysis, 16 Mar 2026, s5).

The groundwork comes first. In 2027 Nigeria and Ghana enter the growth model, because the two highest-spending African markets have no targets yet (section 4.3). Premium activation and the capacity case on the five full regional routes start in 2028, so that seats and demand grow together.

The two-market approach matches the lever to the demand. On the five full regional routes, volume is capped by seats, so the capacity case is where it grows. Premium demand in Nigeria and Kenya already knows South Africa, which ranks second only to Dubai in Kenyan outbound consideration (Skift African Market Analysis, 16 Mar 2026, s4.3). Activation converts that awareness rather than having to create it. Conferences with leisure extensions serve both, because business travel can help smooth demand across the calendar and event attendance can become longer stays (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p17, p41).

Kenya splits its demand in a similar way. Regional African markets drive its volume and business travel, while long-haul markets bring leisure demand and higher spend per visitor (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p32). It draws 41% of its arrivals from Africa, mainly from Uganda and Tanzania (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p32). Nairobi serves as East Africa's aviation, diplomatic and business hub through Kenya Airways' regional network (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p34). The transferable changes are to treat MICE as a system lever and to align city, provincial and national actors around one gateway strategy (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p35). The condition is seats and visas. Activation in Nigeria and Kenya converts only travellers who can get a visa and a seat.
